title: Modern Benoni: unbalanced pawns and the two plans
outcomes: Counts the pawns on each wing after 5...d6 6.e4 g6 and names which side has the majority on files a to d and on files e to h

Finds White's e4-e5 break in the Four Pawns Attack, where a pawn on f4 defends e5, checks it against the engine in a Classical position where the f-pawn is still on f2 and e5 is rated clearly worse, and sees that a defender is a condition to check, not a guarantee
Prepares Black's ...b5 with a knight on c7 and checks what attacks b5 (White's pawn on a4) before pushing
Recognises a position where the structure is absent (5.Nxd5 lines) and one where the e5 plan has to wait

steps.text: **Modern Benoni.** Moves: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e6 (ECO A60 in our data; 2,347 visits in our online sample). After 4.Nc3 exd5 5.cxd5 d6 6.e4 g6 the pawns are unbalanced: White has more pawns on files e to h, Black more on files a to d, and Black has no e-pawn. Each side plays where it has more. Step through one main line, then count.

steps.caption: Position after 5...d6, White to move. Step through one main line. Other moves exist; this line shows how the structure arises.

line.say: 6.e4 builds the centre: White now has pawns on d5 and e4.
...g6 prepares the bishop. Black has no e-pawn any more, so the e-file is half-open for Black.
Bg7 puts the bishop on the long diagonal.
Re8 puts the rook on the half-open e-file, where it attacks the pawn on e4.
Nd2 heads for c4 and defends the pawn on e4.
Na6 brings the knight toward the queenside.
f3 defends the pawn on e4 with a pawn.
Nc7 covers b5, the square Black's break needs.
Black answers ...b6. A later item checks why not ...b5 at once.

claims.statement: After e4 the white pawn stands on e4.
After ...g6 the e-file is half-open for Black (no black e-pawn, a white pawn on e4).
After Re8 the rook attacks e4.
After Nd2 the knight covers c4 and defends e4.
After f3 the pawn on f3 defends e4.
After Nc7 the knight covers b5.
After a4 the pawn on a4 attacks b5.
At the end Black's majority pawns are a7, b6, c5, d6.
At the end White's majority pawns are e4, f3, g2, h2.

steps.text: **What was played (results of games, not evaluations).** Masters (both players 2500 or more, 329,379 games in our file): after 5...d6, 6.e4 in 313 games and 6.Nf3 in 236. After 6.e4 g6 the seventh move was f4 in 145 games (White won 69, drew 49, lost 27), Nf3 in 57 (29, 18, 10), h3 in 49 (20, 21, 8). Online (4,752,291 games): 7.Nf3 appears in 390 games, 7.f4 in 264.

**White's plan: e5 (rule of thumb).** White's extra pawns are in the centre and on the kingside; the break is e4-e5, which attacks d6 and f6. Condition: a pawn should defend e5 after the push. After 7.f4 Bg7 8.Nf3 O-O (the Four Pawns Attack, ECO A68) the pawn on f4 does that. Masters: at 9.Be2 Re8, all 8 games continued 10.e5, a small sample. Find White's move next.

**Black's plan: ...b5 (rule of thumb).** Black's extra pawns are on files a to d; the break is ...b5, and the rook on the half-open e-file adds pressure on e4. Condition: the break needs support first, here a knight on c7. Masters, after 10.Nd2: Nbd7 49 games, Na6 30, a6 8 (87 games); after 11.f3, Nc7 in all 13. Find the preparing move next.

**Check before you push (rule of thumb).** A plan tells you which move to look for, not whether it works now. Ask what attacks the square before pushing, and count attackers against defenders. In the line you stepped through, b5 is attacked by the pawn on a4, the knight on c3 and the bishop on e2, and defended by the knight on c7. The engine's verdict on the tempting pawn push is in the next item.

**When each plan works (rule of thumb).** In the Four Pawns positions here a pawn on f4 defends e5, and e5 is within 0.7 pawn of the best move in two of three; with a black knight on d7 it is not. In one Classical position (f-pawn on f2, rook on e8) e5 is more than 0.7 pawn worse. A defender is a condition to check, not a guarantee. ...b5 needs support and a look at what attacks it. The engine decides each case. Next, three positions: predict, then check.

steps.title: Three positions, one engine question
steps.prompt: White considers e5 in three positions. In the first and third White has played f4 and Black's ninth move is Bg4 or Na6. In the second White has castled with the f-pawn still on f2, Black's rook is on e8 and several things differ at once. Predict each, then check.
Think about the positions you played without hints. Before you chose a move, what did you check? Write one line for each side.
